drills.title: Unsmooth one quarter
drills.question: An appraisal index returned +1.0% last quarter and -0.5% this quarter. With smoothing parameter a = 0.6, what market-value return does the Geltner filter imply for this quarter (%)?
common_mistakes: Dividing by a instead of 1 - a
Adding rather than subtracting the lagged term
Treating the -0.5% appraisal return as the market return
drills.intuition: The appraisal return is a weighted average of this quarter's market return and last quarter's appraisal return; removing the stale part and rescaling reveals a larger move.
drills.takeaway: Small negative appraisal returns after positive ones can hide a sharp market decline. Report the result at two values of a.

drills.title: Roll spread from an autocovariance
drills.question: The first-order autocovariance of trade-to-trade price changes in a stock is -0.0004 ($^2). The midpoint is $25.00. What is Roll's spread estimate in dollars and as a percent of the midpoint?
drills.solution: S = 2 sqrt(0.0004) = 2 x 0.02 = $0.04. As a percent: 0.04/25 = 0.16%. A round trip costs about the full spread, 0.16%.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the factor of 2
Taking the square root of a positive covariance as if it were valid
Calling the half-spread the round-trip cost
drills.intuition: Bid-ask bounce makes successive price changes negatively correlated; the size of that negative correlation reveals the spread.
drills.takeaway: The estimator needs long samples and fails when price changes are positively autocorrelated.

drills.title: CPI surprise to bond and cap rate
drills.question: Core CPI prints 0.4% m/m against a 0.2% consensus. The sd of past surprises is 0.1 pp and the 10-year yield moves 5 bp per 1-sd surprise. Modified duration is 8.0. If 40% of a sustained yield move passes through to a 6.00% cap rate, give: the yield change (bp), the 10-year price change (%), and the eventual property value change (%).
common_mistakes: Using the raw surprise (0.2 pp) instead of the standardized one
Assuming full pass-through to cap rates
Expecting appraisals to show the move this quarter
drills.intuition: Only the surprise relative to expectations moves prices; CRE values react later and partially.
drills.takeaway: Convert surprise to z, z to yield, yield to price; then ask whether positioning differed from consensus.

drills.title: Losing the financed bidders
drills.question: Four bidders for a building with $2.0m NOI value it at cap rates of 4.50% and 4.75% (both levered buyers using bridge debt), 5.00% and 5.25% (unlevered). In an ascending auction, what is the clearing price before and after the two levered bidders lose their financing and exit, and what is the percentage change?
drills.solution: Reservation prices: 44.44m, 42.11m, 40.00m, 38.10m. Price = second highest: $42.11m (implied cap 4.75%). After exits: 40.00m and 38.10m; price = $38.10m (5.25%). Change = 38.095/42.105 - 1 = -9.52%.
common_mistakes: Using the highest bid as the price
Averaging all bidders' valuations
Concluding that NOI or required returns must have changed
drills.intuition: The second-highest bidder sets the price. Remove the top two and the price drops to the old fourth-highest valuation.
drills.takeaway: Ask who will be marginal at closing and what financing they depend on.

drills.title: REITs down 25%, appraisals flat
drills.question: Listed office REITs are down 25% over a year; an appraisal-based index of similar offices is down 2%. Give three explanations for the gap and the evidence that would discriminate between them. What would you not conclude?

rubric: Appraisal lag/smoothing: private values have fallen but appraisals lag; check transaction cap rates, unsmoothed series, volume collapse
REIT-specific factors: leverage, management, development exposure, sentiment or fund outflows; compare REIT-implied cap rates with transaction cap rates and REIT balance sheets
Composition: different property quality, markets, lease terms; compare holdings
Frozen market: few trades because bids are below sellers' reserves; volume data
Does not call the gap an arbitrage and does not assume either number is 'right'

drills.solution: Appraisal smoothing and evidence lag, REIT-specific leverage and sentiment, and composition differences can each produce the gap. Transaction cap rates and volumes discriminate between lag and REIT overreaction; holdings comparison addresses composition. The gap cannot be traded as an arbitrage: private real estate cannot be shorted and there is no convergence date.
common_mistakes: Treating the appraisal index as a price
Treating the REIT price as the private value without adjusting for leverage
Calling the gap a riskless trade
drills.intuition: Public markets move first; appraisals follow transactions with a lag; claims differ.
drills.takeaway: Use REITs as a lead indicator of direction, transactions as a check on size, appraisals as a lagging record.

drills.title: Restating stale comps
drills.question: Subject NOI $1.8m. Three comps sold at 5.00%, 5.30%, 5.60% when a value index stood at 100, 96, 92; it is 90 now. Comps are one class better than the subject (+25 bp). Give the naive average-cap value, the time-adjusted average cap (%), and the time- and quality-adjusted value.
common_mistakes: Averaging unadjusted caps
Adjusting caps in the wrong direction (multiplying by I_now/I_sale)
Forgetting the quality premium
Ignoring that the index itself may understate the decline (selection)
drills.intuition: A comp is a past auction under past financing; restate it to today and to the subject.
drills.takeaway: In a falling market, stale comps support the seller's price. Restate before you rely on them.

drills.title: Price a hotel with no usable evidence

inputs.comps: one REO sale, one sale 20 months ago

drills.question: A broker wants a firm price in three days for a 110-room hotel. The appraisal is 12 months old. The only comps are an REO sale last quarter and a sale 20 months ago. STR shows the comp set's RevPAR down 8%; the seller's P&L shows the subject up 3%. No PIP estimate. Lodging REITs are down 20%. What do you do?

rubric: Declines to give a firm price on this evidence (abstention or non-binding range with conditions is the best answer)
Identifies the STR/P&L conflict as the first item to resolve, with a specific test (STR penetration indices, bank deposits, tax filings)
Treats the REO comp as a forced-sale lower bound and the 20-month comp as stale
Uses the REIT decline as a directional signal, not a price
Lists the information that would allow a bid (reconciled NOI, PIP letter, lender quote) and walk-away triggers

drills.solution: Abstain from a firm price. Offer a wide, non-binding range conditional on reconciling the STR data with the P&L, receiving a PIP estimate and obtaining a lender quote. Treat the REO sale as a floor and the old sale as stale. A bid made to stay in the process on unreconciled NOI is a bet on the seller's honesty.
common_mistakes: Averaging the two comps
Using the appraisal as a price
Bidding firm to stay in the process
drills.intuition: Where no price evidence is usable, the value of waiting for information exceeds the value of speed.
drills.takeaway: Abstention is a decision. Write down what would change it.

drills.title: Clear a small call auction
drills.question: Buy limits: $10.30 x 10, $10.20 x 20, $10.10 x 30. Sell limits: $10.00 x 15, $10.10 x 20, $10.20 x 25. Find the clearing price, executed volume, and imbalance (demand minus supply).
common_mistakes: Choosing the price where D equals S on a continuous interpolation
Counting buy orders with limits below the price as demand
Picking the midpoint of best bid and ask
drills.intuition: The auction price maximizes the volume that can trade; excess demand is left unfilled at that price.
drills.takeaway: Auction prices aggregate orders; a market order shifts the whole schedule.
